main.title: Grim Fandango
main.subtitle: Even the Afterlife Has a Service Counter
main.summary: On October 30, 1998, Grim Fandango reached US stores for Windows, after LucasArts had begun shipping it in the preceding days.

cards.heading: Manny enters the Land of the Dead
cards.text: Grim Fandango reached US Windows stores on October 30, 1998, after LucasArts had begun shipping it in the preceding days. Tim Schafer's adventure follows Manny Calavera through a Land of the Dead shaped by Mexican folklore, Día de Muertos imagery and film noir. Three-dimensional characters move through pre-rendered backgrounds, while dialogue, puzzles and Peter McConnell's music establish the setting's mixture of bureaucracy, humour and melancholy.

cards.heading: Folklore, architecture and noir
cards.text: Skeletal figures evoke Día de Muertos, while offices, casinos, vehicles and buildings draw on modernist forms, Mesoamerican motifs and noir lighting. The afterlife has transport, workplaces and an economy, giving those influences practical roles within its world. Manny remains a clear silhouette as the story moves between places with different architectural styles and atmospheres.

cards.heading: Pointing with Manny’s head
cards.text: Grim Fandango uses direct keyboard control for its three-dimensional characters within pre-rendered scenes. Manny turns his head toward objects that can be examined, signalling interactions through animation. Fixed camera views and changing directions could also make orientation difficult. The interface represented a substantial change from the visible verbs and mouse pointing of earlier LucasArts adventures.

cards.heading: Puzzles within the story
cards.text: Puzzles grow from Manny's efforts to obtain information, convince someone or reach a place. Several require connected actions involving objects and relationships established in the setting. GameSpot's 1998 review highlighted their integration into the plot. A solution can reveal how a character behaves or how the afterlife's institutions work, allowing comedy to emerge during the process.

cards.heading: The humour of a weary professional
cards.text: Contemporary reviews drew connections with Casablanca, Chinatown and Glengarry Glen Ross. Manny's weary professional manner fits a story of ambitions, betrayal and corruption, even within its fantastical setting. Supporting characters have their own goals and speech patterns. The cast's serious treatment of the absurd institutions around them supplies much of the humour.

cards.heading: McConnell’s music and the voice cast
cards.text: Peter McConnell's score draws on jazz and mariachi, helping distinguish cities and situations. Tony Plana voices Manny within a cast whose delivery supports the mixture of comedy and melancholy. The original credits also identify the sound department and LucasArts' iMUSE system for interactive music. Voices, effects and score give places such as Rubacava and El Marrow different sonic identities.

cards.heading: Recovering the production materials
cards.text: While making Remastered, Double Fine recovered diaries, production materials and testimony from the original team. These included notes Schafer wrote in 1998 for the official strategy guide. Finding assets and consulting former collaborators helped reconstruct the game's production. The surviving documents describe the practical decisions and tools behind its images, controls and sound.

main.title: Colony Wars: Vengeance
main.subtitle: Fight from the other side of the war
main.summary: Colony Wars: Vengeance is Psygnosis's PlayStation space-combat game, first released in North America on 3 November 1998. The sequel follows Mertens, a pilot in the Colonial Navy, changing sides from the viewpoint established by the original. Missions place the player in starfighters equipped for particular tasks, with results affecting the route through the campaign. Victory and defeat therefore do more than end an individual sortie. They help determine which part of the larger conflict the player encounters next, giving the pilot's performance consequences beyond a score or a completed objective.

cards.heading: Fight from the other side of the war
cards.text: Colony Wars: Vengeance is Psygnosis's PlayStation space-combat game, first released in North America on 3 November 1998. The sequel follows Mertens, a pilot in the Colonial Navy, changing sides from the viewpoint established by the original. Missions place the player in starfighters equipped for particular tasks, with results affecting the route through the campaign. Victory and defeat therefore do more than end an individual sortie. They help determine which part of the larger conflict the player encounters next, giving the pilot's performance consequences beyond a score or a completed objective.

cards.heading: Use the equipment for the assignment
cards.text: Different starfighters carry combinations of energy weapons, missiles and torpedoes, while some tasks require nonlethal EMP attacks or a grapple to capture an important target. Countermeasures offer a response to incoming missiles. The player must identify what the mission asks for and use the available systems accordingly, rather than treating every object in space as something to destroy. Collected power pods improve attributes such as manoeuvrability and shield capacity. Those upgrades connect completed sorties to the handling of the next one, giving progress a practical effect within the cockpit.

cards.heading: The conflict reaches planetary skies
cards.text: Vengeance adds missions inside planetary atmospheres, widening the series beyond its original space engagements. The campaign also introduces large League machines known as Sentinels, giving the pilot another scale of opponent to confront. Stephen Murphy composed the score for a story still organised around the consequences of success and failure. European release followed later in November 1998. Its most important change is the viewpoint itself: a continuing fictional war becomes less settled when the player takes the controls of a pilot serving the force that previously stood on the other side.

main.title: Crash Bandicoot: Warped
main.summary: Crash Bandicoot: Warped, known in Europe as Crash Bandicoot 3: Warped, is a 1998 platform game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: Crash and Coco travel through time
cards.text: Crash Bandicoot: Warped, known in Europe as Crash Bandicoot 3: Warped, is a 1998 platform game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. It is the third game in the Crash Bandicoot video game series following Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back. The game's story takes place immediately after the events of the second game. When the ruins of Doctor Neo Cortex's space station crash-land on Earth, they unleash an evil entity known as Uka Uka, Aku Aku's evil twin brother, who joins with Cortex and the time-obsessed Doctor Nefarious Tropy as they plan to gather powerful crystals that lay scattered across time, and use their energy to enslave the Earth. The game follows the main characters Crash and Coco Bandicoot as they travel through time and prevent the villains from gathering the crystals by collecting them themselves.

cards.heading: An international PlayStation success
cards.text: Crash Bandicoot: Warped was lauded by critics, who noted a high quality in many areas, including gameplay, graphics and audio, and the game has been considered one of the best video games of all time. It went on to sell nearly 6 million units, making it one of the best-selling video games for the PlayStation. In Japan, the game surpassed the sales of its two predecessors and became the first non-Japanese PlayStation title to sell over 1 million copies in the country. A remastered version was released as a part of the Crash Bandicoot N. Sane Trilogy in 2017. A sequel, Crash Bandicoot 4: It's About Time, was released in 2020.

main.title: Half-Life
main.subtitle: Gordon Freeman crosses Black Mesa
main.summary: On November 19, 1998, Valve releases Half-Life for Windows PC.

cards.heading: An accident inside Black Mesa
cards.text: Valve released Half-Life for Windows on November 19, 1998. Gordon Freeman moves through Black Mesa as an accident transforms the research facility. Events and conversations unfold around the player within the first-person view. Combat, environmental puzzles and traversal vary the pace, supported by Valve's extensively modified Quake-derived technology, scripting, animation and artificial intelligence.

cards.heading: Events unfold around the player
cards.text: The opening tram ride introduces Black Mesa through its rooms, announcements and workers while the player can look around. After the accident, machinery failures, opening doors and reactions from scientists or guards continue to advance events within the level. Scripting gives these encounters timing while leaving Gordon within the same first-person space.

cards.heading: A connected research facility
cards.text: Laboratories connect to offices, rail systems, service areas, ducts and industrial equipment. These spaces suggest a working complex larger than Gordon's immediate route. Elevators can provide pauses or surprises, while ventilation ducts offer shortcuts and more confined encounters. The connected infrastructure helps the game move between exploration, puzzles and combat without abandoning the facility's setting.

cards.heading: Different enemies demand different responses
cards.text: Headcrabs, ranged attacks from vortigaunts and barnacles hanging from ceilings pose different threats. Human soldiers bring grenades, cover and group pressure. Weapons also serve different distances and situations, from the crowbar to explosives and alien devices. Combining enemies with the shape of a room and available resources gives individual encounters their character.

cards.heading: The soldiers announce their actions
cards.text: HECU soldiers move to seek firing angles, throw grenades to dislodge Gordon and communicate through short radio lines. These visible and audible actions make encounters feel like fights against a reacting group. Their effect depends on the combined work of behaviour, animation, sound and the surrounding level, allowing the player to recognise what the soldiers appear to be doing.

cards.heading: Machinery, voices and musical cues
cards.text: Machinery, alarms, footsteps, creatures and weapons supply much of Black Mesa's sound. Kelly Bailey's music enters at selected moments to emphasise a transition or add energy. Scientists and guards provide information, while soldier radio calls and alien noises help identify nearby threats. Sounds beyond a door or around a corner can give the player useful warnings before the source is visible.

cards.heading: Tools for a modding community
cards.text: Valve's tools and SDK allowed players to create new maps and rules around Half-Life's technology. Counter-Strike began as a mod in 1999, demonstrating how far community projects could develop from that foundation. Valve subsequently supported some of these projects officially. The modding community extended the original game's life while establishing new identities and ways to play.

main.title: Tomb Raider III
main.summary: Tomb Raider III (also known as Tomb Raider III: Adventures of Lara Croft) is an action-adventure video game developed by Core Design and published by Eidos Interactive.

cards.heading: Lara follows four meteorite fragments
cards.text: Tomb Raider III (also known as Tomb Raider III: Adventures of Lara Croft) is an action-adventure video game developed by Core Design and published by Eidos Interactive. It was first released for PlayStation and Microsoft Windows in 1998, and for Mac OS in 1999. It is the third title in the Tomb Raider series, following Tomb Raider II (1997). The story follows archaeologist-adventurer Lara Croft as she embarks upon a quest to recover four pieces of a meteorite that are scattered across the world. To progress through the game, the player must complete a series of levels that involve solving puzzles, traversing dangerous locations, and defeating enemies.

cards.heading: New geometry, a return to puzzles
cards.text: Tomb Raider III was built on an upgraded version of the Tomb Raider engine that was used by its predecessors. The engine offers better speed efficiency and new graphical features such as coloured lighting and triangular polygons, allowing developers to achieve greater detail and more complex geometry. The game was designed to be more in line with the puzzle-solving gameplay of the original Tomb Raider as opposed to the more shooting-oriented style of Tomb Raider II.

cards.heading: Success, criticism and The Lost Artefact
cards.text: Accompanied by an extensive marketing campaign, Tomb Raider III was a commercial success, selling around six million copies worldwide. Although the game received generally favourable reviews, it did not fare as well as its predecessors, with critics generally agreeing that the game failed to change the same tried and tested formula. The game's difficult and unforgiving gameplay also received some criticism. A sequel, Tomb Raider: The Last Revelation, was released in 1999. A stand-alone expansion for Tomb Raider III featuring six new levels, subtitled The Lost Artefact, was released in 2000. A remastered version of the game, alongside The Lost Artefact, was included in Tomb Raider I–III Remastered in 2024.

main.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
main.summary: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a 1998 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.

cards.text: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a 1998 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It was the first Legend of Zelda game with 3D graphics. It was released in Japan and North America in November 1998 and in PAL regions the following month.

Ocarina of Time was developed by Nintendo's Entertainment Analysis & Development division. It was led by five directors, including Eiji Aonuma and Yoshiaki Koizumi, produced by series co-creator Shigeru Miyamoto, and written by Kensuke Tanabe. Series composer Koji Kondo wrote its soundtrack. The player controls Link in the realm of Hyrule on a quest to stop the evil king Ganondorf by traveling through time and navigating dungeons and an overworld. The game introduced features such as a target-lock system and context-sensitive buttons, which have since become common in 3D adventure games. The player must play songs on an ocarina to progress.

Ocarina of Time was acclaimed by critics, who praised its visuals, sound, gameplay, soundtrack, and writing. It has been ranked by numerous publications as one of the greatest video games and is the highest-rated game on the review aggregators Metacritic and GameRankings. It set a record for video game pre-orders in the US and sold more than seven million copies worldwide.

Ocarina of Time has been rereleased on every Nintendo home console and on the iQue Player in China. Some releases include Master Quest, an alternative version including new puzzles and increased difficulty. A sequel, Majora's Mask, was released for the Nintendo 64 in 2000. A remake for the Nintendo 3DS, Ocarina of Time 3D, was released in 2011. A second remake for the Nintendo Switch 2 is scheduled to release on November 5th, 2026.

main.title: Nancy Drew: Secrets Can Kill
main.summary: Secrets Can Kill is the first installment in the Nancy Drew point-and-click adventure game series, released on November 23, 1998 by HeR Interactive.

cards.text: Secrets Can Kill is the first installment in the Nancy Drew point-and-click adventure game series, released on November 23, 1998 by HeR Interactive. Players take on the first-person view of fictional amateur sleuth Nancy Drew and solve the mystery through interrogation of suspects, solving puzzles, and discovering clues. The game features pre-rendered 3D environments, but unlike later games, the characters are animated in 2D. There are three levels of gameplay: Junior, Senior, and Master detective modes. Each mode offers a different difficulty level of puzzles and hints, however, none of these changes affect the actual plot of the game. The game is loosely based on a Nancy Drew Files book of the same name, Secrets Can Kill (1986).
An enhanced remake of the game, subtitled Remastered, was released on August 24, 2010. Sales of the original Secrets Can Kill were discontinued on August 1, 2010.

main.title: The Last Blade 2
main.subtitle: A darker return
main.summary: The Last Blade 2 is SNK's weapon-based fighting sequel, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 25 November 1998.

cards.heading: A darker return
cards.text: The Last Blade 2 is SNK's weapon-based fighting sequel, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 25 November 1998. Returning fighters and newcomers continue the supernatural conflict within the late-Edo setting, presented with a darker mood and longer story sequences. The underlying system retains the Power and Speed styles of the first game, allowing the player to choose between heavier damage and connected attacks. Differences between the characters' strengths and weaknesses give that choice another context, encouraging a suitable approach for the fighter and opponent involved.

cards.heading: Combining the two styles
cards.text: An additional EX mode combines elements of Power and Speed, extending the available ways to organise a character's offence. Deflection remains part of handling an incoming attack, so a sequence of strikes still carries the risk of being interrupted by a well-timed reply. The styles provide a framework, while distance and observation decide when an opportunity is safe to use. A familiar fighter can consequently feel different under another selection, with the same visual weapon supporting a different balance between a single damaging blow and a more elaborate exchange.

cards.heading: A confrontation given room to breathe
cards.text: The presentation gives the final conflict more time through extended scenes and subdued colours, maintaining the series' attention to the setting around each duel. Neo Geo CD and later Dreamcast editions added material such as galleries and voiced scenes, while the original arcade game kept the fighting at the centre. The sequel's lasting appeal comes from that balance of atmosphere and precision. Its richly composed stages establish a place and a mood, then leave the players to resolve the encounter through movement, defensive timing and the chosen style's possibilities.

main.title: Dreamcast
main.subtitle: A modem beside the television
main.summary: Sega put network communication inside the console and made connected play part of its identity.

cards.heading: A modem in the living room
cards.text: Dreamcast launched in Japan on 27 November 1998. Its built-in modem supported a vision of browsing, communication and online games from the living room. The Visual Memory unit added a tiny display to the familiar memory card.

cards.heading: An idea outlives its hardware
cards.text: Its library joined arcade traditions to experiments such as Shenmue, Seaman and Phantasy Star Online. Sega ended production and withdrew from making home consoles, but the system's ideas travelled beyond its commercial life.

cards.heading: Arcade DNA and online play
cards.text: A team led by Hideki Sato began developing the Dreamcast in 1997. In contrast to the expensive hardware of the unsuccessful Saturn, the Dreamcast was designed to reduce costs with off-the-shelf components, including a Hitachi SH-4 CPU and an NEC PowerVR2 GPU. The Dreamcast shared hardware with Sega's NAOMI system board, enabling authentic arcade game conversions. Sega used the GD-ROM disc format to avoid the expense of DVD licensing. Developers could use a custom version of Windows CE for easier PC game porting. The Dreamcast was the first console to include a built-in modular modem for internet access and online play.

cards.heading: A final console launch
cards.text: Though its Japanese release was beset by supply problems, the Dreamcast had a successful US launch backed by a large marketing campaign. However, sales steadily declined as Sony built anticipation for the PlayStation 2. Dreamcast sales did not meet Sega's expectations, and attempts to renew interest through price cuts caused significant financial losses. After a change in leadership, Sega discontinued the Dreamcast on March 31, 2001, and restructured itself as a third-party developer. 9.13 million Dreamcasts were sold worldwide and over 600 games were produced. Sega subsequently ported many Dreamcast games to other platforms.

cards.heading: An enduring homebrew community
cards.text: The Dreamcast's commercial failure has been attributed to several factors, including competition from the PlayStation 2, limited third-party support, and the earlier failures of the 32X and Saturn having tarnished Sega's reputation. In retrospect, reviewers have celebrated the Dreamcast as one of the greatest consoles. It is considered ahead of its time for pioneering concepts such as online play and downloadable content. Many Dreamcast games are regarded as innovative, including Sonic Adventure (1998), Crazy Taxi (1999), Shenmue (1999), Jet Set Radio (2000), and Phantasy Star Online (2000). The Dreamcast remains popular in the video game homebrew community, which has developed private servers to preserve its online functions and unofficial Dreamcast software.

cards.heading: A save with its own screen
cards.text: The VMU could display information while seated in the controller and, in supported games, carry small experiences away from the television. Saving was no longer its only visible role. The accessory suggested a relationship between screens, letting a fragment of a larger game acquire its own portable presence.

main.title: Thief: The Dark Project
main.summary: Thief: The Dark Project is a 1998 stealth video game developed by Looking Glass Studios and published by Eidos Interactive for Microsoft Windows.

cards.heading: Garrett enters the City
cards.text: Thief: The Dark Project is a 1998 stealth video game developed by Looking Glass Studios and published by Eidos Interactive for Microsoft Windows. Set in a fantasy metropolis called the City, players take on the role of Garrett, a master thief trained by a secret society who, while carrying out a series of robberies, becomes embroiled in a complex plot that ultimately sees him attempting to prevent a great power from unleashing chaos on the world.

cards.heading: Light and sound guide stealth
cards.text: Thief was the first PC stealth game to use light and sound as game mechanics, and combined complex artificial intelligence with simulation systems to allow for emergent gameplay. The game is notable for its use of first-person perspective for non-confrontational gameplay, which challenged the first-person shooter market and led the developers to call it a "first-person sneaker". Its mechanics were influential on the immersive sim genre as well as later stealth games such as Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell and Hitman.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: The game received critical acclaim and has been placed on numerous hall-of-fame lists, achieving sales of half a million units by 2000, making it Looking Glass' most commercially successful game. It is regarded as one of the greatest video games of all time and helped popularize the stealth genre. Thief was followed by an expanded edition entitled Thief Gold (1999) which modified certain missions and included a few brand new levels. The series continued with two sequels: Thief II: The Metal Age (2000), and Thief: Deadly Shadows (2004), as well as a reboot of the series, Thief (2014). Thief was one of two games in the series that Looking Glass worked on before its closure in 2000. A remastered version of the game, published by Nightdive Studios, is scheduled for release in Winter 2026.
